planting.note: Plant container stock on slopes or banks in spring to establish roots before summer heat; excellent for erosion control.

directions: This Western Australian native forms a dense, mounding mat of fine gray-green foliage that spreads rapidly across slopes and banks, making it a workhorse erosion-control planting throughout Southern California and Arizona landscapes. Clusters of small pale-yellow puffball flowers appear from late winter into spring, attracting bees but producing little litter. Once established it thrives on little to no irrigation and tolerates poor, rocky soils, wind, and reflected heat. Avoid overwatering or rich soil, which encourages leggy growth and shortens the plant's lifespan.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; tolerates both heavy clay and sandy soils once established.

directions: Named for the dense masses of small, fragrant white flowers that smother the canopy in early to midsummer, giving the tree the appearance of a late snowfall. The multi-trunked form develops thick, spongy, pale cream bark that peels in papery layers, providing striking winter interest alongside narrow, needle-like gray-green leaves. It adapts to both wet, poorly drained sites and dry garden conditions, making it unusually versatile for street tree and rain garden plantings in mild climates. Light, structural pruning when young helps develop the attractive multi-trunk habit prized by landscapers.

planting.note: Plant in full sun with good drainage; excellent choice for coastal gardens exposed to salt spray and wind.

directions: A rounded Western Australian shrub or small tree prized for its summer-to-fall show of fuzzy, rose-pink to lavender pompom flower clusters set against gray-green leathery leaves. It is one of the more salt- and wind-tolerant melaleucas, performing reliably in exposed coastal and seaside plantings where few other flowering shrubs persist. Established plants need minimal supplemental water and benefit from occasional tip pruning after bloom to maintain a dense, compact form. Avoid heavy, poorly drained soils, which can lead to root rot.

planting.note: Space plants for hedging or windbreak use; tolerates heavy pruning and shearing.

directions: This fast-growing southeastern Australian native carries fine, needle-like foliage on a dense, upright frame, making it one of the most reliable evergreen windbreak and privacy-screen shrubs for mild-winter climates. Creamy-white bottlebrush-like flower spikes line the branch tips in late summer and fall, drawing bees and small nectar-feeding birds. It tolerates poor, shallow, or compacted soils and withstands hard pruning or shearing into formal hedges without loss of vigor. Once established it needs little irrigation and is rarely bothered by pests.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil; one of the most cold-tolerant eucalyptus species for marginal zones.

directions: A multi-stemmed mallee eucalyptus from the Victorian and New South Wales high country, valued by cold-climate gardeners for its unusual tolerance of hard frost and occasional snow. Juvenile foliage is glossy, rounded, and blue-green, held on an open, naturally multi-trunked framework that rarely needs staking. It performs best in well-drained soil and full sun, and resents waterlogged roots far more than it minds cold. Light thinning of competing stems in youth encourages a more open, tree-like silhouette over time.

planting.note: Plant in a sheltered site with sharp drainage; valued as one of the hardiest eucalyptus for colder zones.

directions: Famous for its smooth, patchwork bark that peels away to reveal streaks of cream, gray, green, and rust, the snow gum is a highland Australian species that handles hard frost and snow loads better than almost any other eucalyptus grown ornamentally. Small clusters of white flowers appear in summer, but the real draw is the sculptural trunk and silvery, sickle-shaped adult leaves that move readily in the wind. It prefers lean, fast-draining soil and resents fertile, wet conditions that favor fungal problems over hardiness. Underplanting with low groundcovers helps showcase the bark, the species' signature feature.

planting.note: Plant in full sun with good drainage; widely grown commercially for cut foliage.

directions: This compact New South Wales species keeps its small, rounded, blue-gray juvenile leaves well into maturity rather than switching to the long, lance-shaped adult foliage typical of most eucalyptus, which makes it a favorite with florists and foliage growers. It forms a dense, rounded crown on a slender trunk and tolerates colder winters than most ornamental gums grown in home gardens. Full sun and sharp drainage keep it compact and healthy; regular coppicing or pollarding is a common technique to keep producing the prized juvenile foliage. It is notably resilient to light frost once past its first winter.

planting.note: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; a popular street and specimen tree in mild climates.

directions: A graceful, weeping New South Wales eucalyptus clothed in fine, willowy, blue-green leaves that release a sharp peppermint fragrance when brushed or crushed. Reddish-brown, deeply furrowed fibrous bark contrasts attractively with the airy, drooping canopy, and small white flower clusters appear intermittently through the year. It is widely planted as a street and specimen tree for its fast growth, drought tolerance, and tidy habit, though it should be given room to develop its naturally pendulous form. Avoid heavy, wet soils, which shorten the tree's lifespan considerably.

planting.note: Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; fast-growing and tolerant of shearing for hedges.

directions: One of the fastest-growing hakeas, this eastern Australian species carries glossy, willow-like leaves on a dense, upright shrub that is widely planted as an informal screen or clipped hedge. Small clusters of creamy-white flowers open in spring, followed by the woody, horned seed capsules typical of the genus. It is notably tolerant of coastal salt spray, wind, and poor sandy soils, but like most Proteaceae it performs poorly in rich, phosphorus-fertilized garden beds. Light shearing after bloom keeps the habit dense and prevents the somewhat leggy growth it can develop if left unpruned.

planting.note: Plant in very lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; do not fertilize with phosphorus.

directions: A striking West Australian shrub with narrow, rigid, grass-like gray-green leaves that give way in winter and early spring to long, dense spikes of vivid pink-to-red flowers held along older wood. The flower spikes are a magnet for honeyeaters and, in cultivation, hummingbirds, providing color during the coldest months when little else is in bloom. Like other hakeas it demands lean, extremely well-drained soil and is highly sensitive to phosphorus fertilizer and wet feet. Minimal pruning is needed beyond removing spent flower spikes to tidy the plant's naturally open, upright form.
